claims.text: Severe plastic deformation of a supersaturated BCC refractory multi-principal-element alloy followed by controlled low-temperature aging can simultaneously produce nanocrystallization and a dual-phase structure.
Coherent B2 or ordered-BCC precipitates produced by this route would be non-brittle.
Composition control and multistage thermomechanical processing can suppress TCP phases while enabling coherent precipitation from a supersaturated matrix.
Cast or homogenized HfNbTaTiZr or W-based refractory alloys can have a coarse, single-phase BCC starting matrix.
Limited ductility in the starting alloy is caused by high lattice friction and the potential formation of brittle phases during cooling.
High-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing can reduce the grain size of the proposed alloys below 50 nm.
A multistage thermomechanical process can nucleate coherent dual nanoprecipitates in a W-based refractory alloy.
Aging must be conducted below the coherent-precipitate solvus but above a threshold for grain growth.
Vacuum or inert-atmosphere processing prevents oxide formation, while uncontrolled oxygen or oxide particles provide a separate strengthening contribution.
The target mediator is a BCC matrix with grains below 50 nm and a high volume fraction of coherent B2 or D0a-type precipitates that do not initiate cracks.
Strengthening would arise synergistically from grain-boundary strengthening, solid-solution strengthening, and coherent-precipitation hardening.
Controlling stoichiometry and aging kinetics can favor coherent ordering over separation into brittle Laves, silicide, or TCP phases.
The proposed alloy will exceed 2000 MPa yield strength, 500 HV hardness, and 10% fracture strain.
Ductility above 10% would be retained because brittle intergranular phases are absent and coherent precipitates are present in a ductile nanocrystalline matrix.
The coarse-grained single-phase BCC baseline typically has yield strength below 1000 MPa and brittle fracture because it lacks grain refinement and precipitation hardening.
The target microstructure becomes unstable above the coherent-precipitate solvus because precipitate coarsening causes loss of strength.
High Cr or Si content can place the alloy in a stability region for brittle Laves or silicide phases.
Oxygen above approximately 0.8 wt% causes oxide formation and significant additional hardening, potentially overriding the intended strengthening mechanism.
The nanocrystalline structure may become unstable above 600 degrees Celsius.
Formation of Laves or silicide phases after severe plastic deformation and aging, or fracture strain below 5% despite the target dual-phase nanostructure, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis initially describes a dual-phase solid-solution structure, but the specified mediator is a solid-solution BCC matrix plus ordered intermetallic B2 or D0a precipitates, not two solid-solution phases.

The conditions require aging above the threshold for grain growth, whereas the intervention and mediator require preservation of grains below 50 nm; operation above a grain-growth threshold would tend to undermine that target.
